subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: The big idea is the data table — a grid with rows and columns. They then learn about data types — the kind of data a field is allowed to hold — and finally how to search a data table to answer real questions, such as “How many items are in the Snacks section?” In Sessions 4 and 5 they move the same skills onto a computer, building a small data table in a free spreadsheet. Most of this unit is unplugged: you draw and label data tables in their notebooks, sort facts by type, and search tables by hand. Alongside the content, you practise two thinking skills from the syllabus: they group items that belong together, and they decide which field to look in before they start a search.

outcomes: Explain that a database is an organised collection of data, and that a data table stores data in rows and columns.
Name and point to the three parts of a data table: field (column), record (row) and data item (one fact in a cell).
Tell the difference between data (raw facts) and information (data that answers a question or has meaning).
Name the main data types — Text, Number, Date/Time and Yes/No — and recognise Currency as the special number type used for money.
Choose the correct data type for a field, including the tricky case where a contact number is stored as Text (because it is not used for sums).
Explain the rule that every cell in one field must use the same data type and format.
Search a data table to answer a question by first choosing the correct field, then scanning, counting or matching.
Enter data into the cells of a spreadsheet in LibreOffice Calc, format the header row, and format a column as currency.
Design a small data table of their own, choose sensible data types, enter records, and write questions the table can answer.

Before this unit (from the syllabus), children should already be able to enter data into the cells of a spreadsheet, format cells, tell data apart from information, and know that a database can be physical (on paper) or digital (on a computer). This unit builds directly on those skills.

concepts.title: Data, data tables, records and fields (unplugged)
concepts.explanation: A database is an organised collection of facts. We keep data organised so we can find it quickly. The tidiest way is a data table — a grid of rows and columns. Check yourself: Can you count the fields and records correctly? Can you see that a record goes across (a row), not down? Can you point to a field, a record and a data item and use the right word for each?
concepts.example: Teach the three parts using the register below: a field is a column (one kind of information, like Age); a record is a row (everything about one child); and a data item is one fact in one cell (like the 9 in Leila's Age cell). Also separate data (raw facts: “Leila”, "9 “) from information (” Leila is 9 years old").
concepts.checkYourself: Can you count the fields and records correctly? Can you see that a record goes across (a row), not down? Can you point to a field, a record and a data item and use the right word for each?

concepts.title: Data types (unplugged)
concepts.explanation: Every field has a data type — the kind of data it is allowed to hold. Teach the four main types: Text (letters and other characters), Number (only numbers, and you can do sums with them), Date/Time (a date or a time), and Yes/No (only one of two values).
concepts.example: Then add Currency as the money type — a Number shown with a money sign like $3.00. The key rule: every cell in one field must use the same data type and format.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you know you cannot do sums on Text? Do you pick Text for a contact number and explain why?

concepts.title: Searching a data table to answer questions (unplugged)
concepts.explanation: People keep data so they can answer questions with it. To search a data table, use two steps: Step 1 — choose the right field (which column has the answer?), then Step 2 — scan, count or match down that field. This “field first” habit is the thinking skill of the unit: decide where to look before you look.
concepts.example: Find one real example of searching a data table to answer questions around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you count matches accurately and read across a record to the right cell? Do you name the field before searching?

concepts.title: From paper to screen: a data table in LibreOffice Calc (on-screen)
concepts.explanation:
The same data table works on a computer, where it is quicker to change and search. Five Friends. Teach that a spreadsheet is a giant grid: columns have letters (A, B, C.), rows have numbers (1, 2, 3.), and each box is a cell with an address like A1. The header row (row 1) holds the field names; each record goes on its own row underneath.

This is exactly the layout you build Model it on the projector, step by step, and have you copy each step.
concepts.example: Find one real example of from paper to screen: a data table in LibreOffice Calc (on-screen) around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you put field names in row 1 and one record per row? Can you remember to save? Can you type into the correct cell?

concepts.title: Be a data boss: your own class database (project)
concepts.explanation:
A data boss can design a data table, choose the right data type for every field, enter records neatly, and then search their table to answer questions.

Books in our class corner. Then invent two records together so they see a record fill up across the row.
concepts.example: Finally, write one search question the table can answer, such as “How many books have more than 100 pages?”, and show which field answers it. Write the data type next to each field before entering any data, so the plan comes first.
concepts.checkYourself: Are the fields sensible and each given a correct data type? Are there at least five complete records? Do the search questions actually match the fields in the table, and are the answers correct?

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

terms: database
An organised collection of data kept in one place.
data table
A grid that stores data in rows and columns.
data
Raw facts and figures, on their own.
information
Data that has meaning or answers a question.
field
A column in a data table — one kind of information.
record
A row in a data table — all the data about one person or thing.
data item
One single fact in one cell.
data type
The kind of data a field is allowed to store.
Currency
The special number type used for money.
format
The way data is arranged or shown.
search
To look through a data table to find an answer.
field first
Choosing which column to look in before you search.

selfAssessment: I can explain that a database is an organised collection of data, and that a data table stores data in rows and columns.
I can name and point to the three parts of a data table: field (column), record (row) and data item (one fact in a cell).
I can tell the difference between data (raw facts) and information (data that answers a question or has meaning).
I can name the main data types — Text, Number, Date/Time and Yes/No — and recognise Currency as the special number type used for money.
I can choose the correct data type for a field, including the tricky case where a contact number is stored as Text (because it is not used for sums).
I can explain the rule that every cell in one field must use the same data type and format.
I can search a data table to answer a question by first choosing the correct field, then scanning, counting or matching.
I can enter data into the cells of a spreadsheet in LibreOffice Calc, format the header row, and format a column as currency.
I can design a small data table of their own, choose sensible data types, enter records, and write questions the table can answer.

I can before this unit (from the syllabus), children should already be able to enter data into the cells of a spreadsheet, format cells, tell data apart from information, and know that a database can be physical (on paper) or digital (on a computer). This unit builds directly on those skills.
